title: The Half Shell
series: The Half Shell, an illustrated essay on oysters
style: Sunlit anime-style watercolour flat-lay seen from above: indigo cloth on a pale wood table, slate and porcelain plates, crushed ice, crisp white gloss dashes, soft diagonal light; Zen Maru Gothic headings, Barlow body, IBM Plex Mono labels.
context: The Half Shell is an illustrated essay on oysters. Thesis: an oyster is a jar of the water it grew in. Oysters are osmoconformers: they match the salinity of the water by filling their cells with free amino acids; taurine is about 80% of the amino acids in Pacific oysters (Zhao et al. 2017, Scientific Reports). Saltier water gives more amino acids and more umami; low-salinity water gives bland oysters (Rice 2019, URI). Sweetness is glycogen, highest before spawning. History: shell ring on St. Catherines Island, Georgia, about 4,300 years old, harvests only in cool months (Florida Museum 2019); Sergius Orata farmed oysters at Lucrine Lake around 95 BCE; Dickens, Pickwick Papers 1836–37: 'poverty and oysters' go together; New York harbor had about 350 sq mi of beds (Kurlansky, estimate); Canal Street Plan: all you can eat for 6 cents; by 1880 NY waters produced about 700 million oysters a year; the last NY bed (Raritan Bay) closed in 1927. Happy hour: Crave Fishbar NYC (2019) charges $3–4 normally, $1–1.50 at happy hour, pays about $0.77–0.80 wholesale, shucks ~20,000 a week, 6,000 at happy hour (Marketplace 2019); Boston 2024 wholesale $0.65–1.15, farm-gate $0.57 (Boston Globe); the deal is a loss leader, drinks and food pay. 19th-century saloon free lunch (La Bourse de Maspero, New Orleans 1838; one free oyster per drink in Chicago); oyster happy hour revived at Shaw's Crab House, Chicago, late 1980s; 'happy hour' from US Navy socials of 1913. Place: briny northern bays (Wellfleet, Island Creek, Moonstone, Malpeque), mild Chesapeake and Gulf (5–15 ppt), Pacific coast cucumber and melon notes (Hama Hama, Kumamoto), European flats metallic, Marennes-Oléron green oysters; a CSIRO trained panel found all 12 sensory attributes differed by region. Season: spawning above ~20°C; Vibrio peaks May–October; CDC estimates 80,000 US vibriosis cases a year, 52,000 foodborne; triploids barely spawn (50% of West Coast farmed Pacifics in 2016). Price: US restaurant average $3.34 (East Coast) to $3.71 (West Coast) per oyster in 2021 menus; Kumamoto $95 per 30 from Taylor Shellfish; Gillardeau N°2 €36 per 6 and wild flat Belons €39 per 6 at Le Dôme, Paris (2026); flat oyster yields fell about 90% after Marteilia (1968) and Bonamia (~1979); Coffin Bay King oysters 6–7 years, ~1 kg, 18 cm, A$100 each (2008–2012). How to tell a good one: closed or closes when tapped (FDA), heavy, full of liquor, smells like the sea, harvest tags kept 90 days after the container is emptied (FDA Food Code), keep at 35–45°F cup down, eat within about a week.
